items.summary: Wireless communication networks are expanding from mere information transfer to sensing: in the Integrated Sensing and Communication paradigm, existing infrastructure and signals are reused to capture physical information about the surroundings of devices, envisioned to inform high-stakes applications such as healthcare and autonomous vehicles. From a security perspective, wireless sensing inherently trusts physical observations of the radio environment. However, as in wireless communication, the open nature of radio propagation allows attackers to tamper with victim signals. In particular, attackers can use programmable metasurfaces to manipulate wireless channels and thereby mislead sensing systems. Yet, prior metasurface-based manipulations target only individual channel features such as variance or Doppler shifts. Thus, they require knowledge of the victim sensing system and produce implausible channels that are easy to detect. In this work, we show that metasurfaces enable physically plausible manipulation of wireless sensing that is independent of the features used by the victim sensing system. Our attack reproduces genuine pre-recorded events at the physical layer and thereby synthesizes physical deepfakes of wireless channels. To this end, we develop an attack framework that controls the amplitude and phase of victim channels across time, frequency, and antennas. The key challenge here is to build a deep learning model of the interaction between metasurface and victim channel. We demonstrate that attackers can solve this challenge in several settings, e.g., by exploiting Wi-Fi Beamforming Feedback Information or replicating the victim environment. We validate the attack both in a controlled lab study on MIMO channels and with off-the-shelf Wi-Fi sensing. Our results fundamentally challenge the trustworthiness of wireless sensing.
items.title: Spoofing Wireless Sensing with Metasurface-based Physical Deepfakes

items.summary: Face Verification (FV) systems have exhibited remarkable performance in verification tasks and have consequently garnered extensive adoption across various applications, from identity duplication to authentication in mobile payments. However, the surge in popularity of face verification has raised concerns about potential vulnerabilities in the face of adversarial attacks. These concerns originate from the fact that advanced FV systems, which rely on deep neural networks, have recently demonstrated susceptibility to crafted input samples known as adversarial examples. Although imperceptible to human observers, adversarial examples can deceive deep neural networks during the testing and deployment phases. These vulnerabilities raised significant concerns about the deployment of deep neural networks in safety-critical contexts, prompting extensive investigations into adversarial attacks and corresponding defense strategies. This comprehensive survey provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in deep face verification, encompassing a broad spectrum of topics such as algorithmic designs, database utilization, protocols, and application scenarios. Furthermore, we conduct an in-depth examination of state-of-the-art algorithms to generate adversarial examples and the defense mechanisms devised to mitigate such adversarial threats.
items.title: A comprehensive survey of deep face verification systems adversarial attacks and defense strategies

items.summary: The spread of fake news among Arabic media including social media represents a great challenge to the integrity of information and the trust of the public in it. In this paper, we introduce a comprehensive deep-learning framework, named ArabFake, that goes beyond the binary classification on Arabic fake news detection. ArabFake, built over MARBERTv2 (a state-of-the-art model for multi-dialectal Arabic tweets), proficiently address the complexity of the Arabic language while performing three unified tasks which are fake news detection, content categorization and its risk assessment. The framework promotes efficiency and performance both by enabling multi-task learning through shared knowledge representation across tasks. In order to facilitate development and evaluation, we present the ArabFake Dataset consisting of 2,495 manually labelled news items with labels that are verified by experts regarding fake news categories and risk levels. ArabFake demonstrates robust performance, achieving an F1 score of 94.12% for fake news detection, 84.92% for categorization, and 88.91% for risk zone assessment, highlighting its reliability and effectiveness across multiple tasks. We improve interpretability and extract insight into manipulative techniques by integrating valence scoring as part of the framework that emphasizes misleading linguistic cues used to disseminate fake news within the produced image. The results show that ArabFake is a holistic Arabic fake news detection framework that has practical implications on news organizations and fact checking projects.
items.title: ArabFake: A multitask deep learning framework for Arabic fake news Detection, Categorization, and risk prediction

items.summary: Cloud-hosted vision-language models (VLMs) require sending images beyond the user's local trust boundary, potentially exposing sensitive information the query does not need. We study query-guided visual minimization: a trusted local transformation preserves query-relevant visual content and reduces unnecessary disclosure before transmission. Unlike query-agnostic anonymization, it preserves the same sensitive content when the query requires it and suppresses it otherwise. We introduce QGVM, a framework that combines query grounding with an independent sensitive-item inventory, determines disclosure necessity at the type, instance, and text-content levels, and renders a minimized image for a black-box downstream VLM. We evaluate QGVM on complementary benchmarks measuring task utility, directly recoverable sensitive information, and inferential geolocation leakage. With OpenAI GPT-6.1 Sol, QGVM achieves 85.3% DoxBench answer correctness versus 77.5% for PGP, while a separately prompted Sol geolocation attacker succeeds within 1 km on 5.8% of QGVM images versus 25.7% of unprotected images. On Scene-Privacy, QGVM reduces face re-identification from 27.7% (PGP) to 4.5%. On held-out BIV-Priv-Seg, unnecessary private-text recovery falls from 33.9% (PGP) to 15.3%. To verify that disclosure is query-dependent, we evaluate paired queries that either require or do not require the same sensitive information. QGVM achieves 69.6% correct disclosure switching, compared with 29.1% for grounding-only cropping. These findings highlight the value of distinguishing visual relevance from disclosure necessity, while revealing the privacy-utility trade-offs of selective visual disclosure.
items.title: Query-Guided Visual Minimization for Selective Disclosure to Cloud VLMs

items.summary: Language models can generate Python that drives industrial protocols on programmable logic controllers, yet existing code-grounding checks ask whether an imported package or symbol exists rather than whether it suits the declared industrial target. We define \emph{metadata-conditioned, import-level vendor--protocol incompatibility} and build \textsc{Proteus-OT}, a label-free static verifier over a version-pinned graph of documented bindings. Across 883 generated scripts, 180 carry an import-level mismatch against the declared target (20.4\%); restricting to single-vendor targets gives 16.3\%, and additionally requiring the offending library to reach a protocol communication call gives 14.2\%, which we read as conditional on the corpus metadata rather than on verified intent. None of the 28 adjudicable human control files carries one, a sample too small to estimate a prevalence. Within the balanced subset, 96.6\% of mismatching scripts import packages and call methods that exist, so an existence baseline does not represent them, and every positive ships with an inspectable witness. We also audit machine-versus-human classification on the same corpus, where character $n$-grams reach macro-F1 1.000 under task, model and vendor-disjoint partitions and survive comment removal, an AST round trip and identifier anonymisation. The trailing newline present in 95.2\% of human files and in none of the generated ones separates the classes on its own. Vendor--protocol consistency is a useful static audit target, whereas provenance classification on repository-labelled corpora is not authorship detection.
items.title: Real Package, Wrong Controller: Static Auditing of Vendor--Protocol Mismatches in LLM-Generated PLC Code

items.summary: Coding agents let plugins and remote services answer permission prompts, and Claude Code documents that such an answer cannot override the operator's deny rules. However, we show that this guarantee, checked one decision at a time, fails over a whole run, because an answer to one permission prompt can rewrite the policy that every later answer is checked against. For example, a remote service with no access to the operator's files approves an unrelated command and attaches an update that deletes the deny rule protecting the project's secrets. The agent then reads the secrets in that session and the next, even inside the vendor's strict sandbox. The root cause is that Claude Code checks only updates that add or replace allow rules. Relays that forward such deletions already exist, including the vendor's own Remote Control. In effect, the right to answer a prompt has become the right to administer the policy. Worse, the deletion leaves the same records as a local edit by the operator, so Claude Code cannot tell who wrote a rule. More generally, what a runtime records decides what it can safely delegate. A runtime that cannot tell who wrote a rule can accept only updates that keep every currently denied call denied, whereas, to protect every party's restrictions, a runtime that records who wrote each rule can let each party remove only the restrictions proven to be its own. We prove that these two bounds are tight. They correctly predict whether the operator's restrictions survive in all thirteen permission designs across ten agent systems, including predictions we wrote down before running Codex, Gemini CLI, opencode, and Goose. Enforcing the bounds at the shared update step blocks the attack. A survey of 2,227 fetched marketplace plugins finds only two that send policy updates.
items.title: When Answering Is Administering: Permission Replies That Rewrite Coding-Agent Policy

items.summary: Request-derived authorizers such as Progent protect LLM agents from prompt injection by deriving what an agent may do from the user's request. Their guarantee rests on attribution: the request is taken to be what the user said. Compaction breaks it. At every automatic compaction we observed, Claude Code and Codex placed a model-written summary of earlier turns as a user message, so the compactor's quotation of the user, documents and injected text reads as the user speaking. Because a policy frozen at the first request lets the agent finish few later tasks, we let Progent derive its policy for each request, and find that what it grants then follows what the compactor wrote. Even a payee the user stated is not safe: when an attacker's notice states another account as plain data and the user asks to pay the rent, the policy derived from a frontier compactor's summary admits the notice's account in 91% of cases, and the one derived from the user's own words in none. The cause is general: we prove that an authorizer that cannot see who wrote which bytes cannot treat a forged record differently from the legitimate one it imitates by more than the two are distinguishable, and that the bound is tight. Frontier compactors bear this out: they mark injected instructions, which have no legitimate twin, but rarely injected data, which does. What a compactor keeps, and how it marks it, is a security parameter. The fix follows from attribution: the authorizer credits only what the user said, authenticated on arrival and carried verbatim across the boundary, while the agent still reads the summary. We prove that it then receives exactly that text or nothing, so an attacker can block the policy but cannot shape it, and adaptive attacks on our implementation confirm it. In 40 attacked AgentDojo episodes re-run with the fix, no attacker action completes while the agent reads the summary.
items.title: LLM Agent Authorization Across Context Compaction

items.summary: Homomorphic encryption enables computation on encrypted data, but its high computational overhead remains a central obstacle. We overcome this obstacle asymptotically for high-precision fixed-point arithmetic. In this paper, we introduce focused encoding, which represents a fixed-point number of $n$-bit precision using a polynomial of degree $O(n/\log n)$ over a polynomially bounded modulus by concentrating precision at one embedding. We then introduce an error-shaping technique for homomorphic operations to preserve the encoding. This yields an encrypted fixed-point multiplication algorithm for the CKKS scheme that runs in online time $O(n \log n)$ at $n$-bit precision for any fixed multiplicative depth, with security parameter $λ= O(n/\log^2 n)$. Further, we develop bootstrapping for focused encoding to overcome the quadratic cost of conventional bootstrapping. We bootstrap ciphertext coefficients at an enlarged scale and shape the resulting error to preserve focused encoding, at the cost of additional modulus consumption. Then, to reduce the remaining logarithmic overhead, we decompose the ciphertext into components over a smaller subring and bootstrap each separately. This reduces the online cost per multiplication, including bootstrapping, to $O(n \log n + n (\log λ)^3 \log \log λ)$ for security parameter $λ= O(n/\log^3 n)$.
items.title: Encrypted Fixed-Point Multiplication in Quasilinear Complexity

items.summary: We show that quantization asymmetry concentrates bit-flip vulnerability in small tensors retained at high precision. CoarseHammer targets these tensors and accepts flips at any bit, without parameter values, gradients, or data. It remains effective under continued fine-tuning. Under ideal placement, CoarseHammer reaches chance accuracy in at least 81.5% of runs on each of ten evaluated models, including four large language models, with median successful runs requiring at most 24 flips. On simulated DRAM with 0.01 flippable bits per million, it outperforms three prior attacks on every evaluated convolutional network, succeeding in up to 83.6% of runs while they never succeed. On a real system, CoarseHammer steers heap-allocated tensors onto vulnerable frames despite address space layout randomization, without accessing the model file. With 16 templated frames, median accuracy reaches chance for all four language models and approximately chance for four convolutional networks.
items.title: Bit-Flip Attacks on Quantized Neural Networks without Knowledge of Model Parameters

items.summary: Programmatic verifiers provide scalable reward signals for training coding agents with reinforcement learning, yet subtle harness defects and incomplete unit tests allow policies to earn full credit without solving the intended task. Existing training-time defenses intervene either by penalizing suspicious outputs or by filtering flagged tasks and rollouts. However, output penalties leave the underlying verifier exploitable, driving policies to disguise shortcuts under reasoning monitors or zeroing out valid solutions under detector false positives, whereas task and rollout filtering discards or mutes the hardest problems where shortcuts emerge earliest. Pre-training verifier hardening repairs the environment directly, but misses vulnerability classes that surface only as the policy improves during reinforcement learning. In this paper, we propose online environment repair, which leaves triggering rollout rewards unchanged to remove hiding incentives and asynchronously patches exploited environments during training. Candidate repairs triggered by execution invariants or differential fuzzing are deployed only after passing three automated validation gates that block the exploit while preserving valid solutions, canceling detector false positives and enabling structural propagation across repositories without scaffold labels or reference solutions. Across 20 controlled GRPO experiments on heterogeneous software-engineering repositories, online environment repair reduces cumulative reward hacking from 36.9% to 0.06% and improves held-out Pass@8 from 21.7% to 46.7%, consistently outperforming reward-penalty, rollout-filtering, and static-hardening baselines while eliminating zero-shot exploitation on unseen loophole classes.
items.title: Online Environment Repair for Coding Agents

items.summary: Long-lived secure channels for embedded and cyber-physical systems (CPSs) must resist quantum attacks and failures in endpoint randomness. While several post-quantum key exchange protocols exist, their security assumes reliable randomness at the endpoint, but this assumption is not always true in embedded devices. In this paper, we introduce the Entropy Attack Suite (EAS) to evaluate secure channels facing endpoint randomness failures, such as low-entropy boot and Random Number Generation (RNG) path subversion. As a case study, we design and implement APQKE-DR, a post-quantum secure channel. Its handshake uses ML-KEM [1] and ML-DSA [2], producing a root key for an X25519 Double Ratchet. We assess the performance of APQKE-DR and security for smart grid communication, and integrate it beneath ANSI C12.22 and DNP3 without altering payload formats. On a Raspberry Pi Compute Module 5, the APQKE handshake exchanges 9,610 bytes with median latencies of 1.99 ms (node) and 0.82 ms (server). The ratcheted channel adds 31 bytes per message. With fresh randomness and ideal cryptographic primitives, ProVerif verifies the modeled secrecy and authentication properties. If randomness fails, EAS can recover the RNG stream and root key from public transcripts. Under RNG-path subversion, a weak generator exposes the root key across sessions. If subversion also affects X25519 keys, attackers may access ratchet keys and plaintexts. TPM seeding prevents early-boot attacks but not later subversion, while measured boot can block modified firmware. Secure deployment thus requires integrity along the entire entropy path, not just strong cryptographic primitives.
items.title: APQKE-DR: Entropy-Failure Analysis of a Post-Quantum-Initialized Ratcheted Channel

items.summary: Circuit breaker, retry, and bulkhead settings in Java microservices are tuned once and frozen, although the best setting depends on the fault a dependency is currently showing. We study whether an online learner can pick these settings at runtime. AdaptR4j swaps Resilience4j policies atomically in Spring Boot 3 and lets a contextual bandit choose among complete CircuitBreaker/Retry/Bulkhead configurations from Prometheus signals. Our first, naive design scored worse than keeping the default policy in three of four winnable fault scenarios under the reward it optimised: exploring a menu that contained aggressive circuit breakers rejected most traffic while the learner was still learning. Two safeguards fix this: a safe policy menu (no breaker stricter than the latency SLO) and safe exploration with a bounded reward. With them, AdaptR4j beats the production default in every winnable scenario (p < 0.001, three runs each, run-to-run SD <= 0.03), beats the best fixed policy when the fault changes over time, and cuts user-visible failures up to 3.7x compared with the naive design. A context-free bandit on the same safe menu performs statistically indistinguishably, so the safeguards - not the learner - carry most of the benefit. We also report how an earlier version of our harness produced convincing but wrong results: a unit mismatch made every circuit breaker 100x too strict and rejected calls were invisible to the metrics, so 94% of user requests failed while latency and error metrics looked excellent.
items.title: When Online Adaptation of Resilience Policies Hurts: Safe Exploration and Measurement Pitfalls in Resilience4j

items.summary: Software vulnerabilities leave systems open to attack, and their remediation is often delayed. Large language models (LLMs) have advanced automated patch generation, yet passing functionality tests does not ensure that a patch enforces the security requirement the vulnerability violated. Existing vulnerability repair techniques rely on curated patterns or templates with limited coverage, leaving unclear which repair strategies carry over across vulnerabilities and how they can steer LLMs. We present a large-scale empirical study that relates recurring fix patterns to the security impacts of vulnerabilities and examines how this knowledge can guide LLM-based repair. Building on a manual study of security patches, we cluster 3,816 security patches from 348 open-source repositories and analyze the edits and their context to derive concrete fix patterns, ranging from local safeguards to coordinated changes across multiple locations. We define 12 security impact classes by the security requirements that vulnerabilities violate and map them to repair categories and fix patterns, revealing characteristic repairs, alternative strategies within a class, and patterns shared across classes. We then use these patterns and impact-pattern associations to select repair examples for four LLMs on repair tasks of varying complexity. Guided example selection raises the four-model mean pass@3 from 37.9% under zero-shot prompting to up to 49.2%, whereas randomly selected examples reach only 36.9%. Our findings connect vulnerability characterization with patch generation and support organizing repair knowledge around security requirements.
items.title: Not Just Any Example: Security Requirements and Fix Patterns for Guiding LLM Vulnerability Repair

items.summary: AI audits have garnered significant attention in recent months, as the ability to test and monitor AI models plays a crucial role in safe development and deployment. However, AI audit success hinges on an auditor's authority; in particular, what information and resources they have at their disposal. Ongoing debates have surrounded the question: How much model access is needed to conduct an AI audit? Auditors seek more model access, while companies resist it for reasons related to confidential business information (trade secrets) and privacy. This tug-of-war remains unresolved. Further, this debate misses a related question: How much data and compute do auditors need? In this work, we systematically investigate both questions. We provide a framework that varies each of these three dimensions-model access, data, and compute-and measures their joint effect on audit success. We apply this framework to three tasks. We find that (1) some model access is important, but there can be diminishing returns; (2) data and compute matter more for traditional fairness audits, but model access matters more for manipulation and lie detection; and (3) these three resources can be fungible (i.e., an exchange rate exists between them), meaning that model access is not the only salient factor. These results suggest that audit governance should jointly consider different dimensions of auditor authority (including model access, data, and compute) in relation to audit objectives. These issues are particularly salient as we consider the spectrum of auditing setups, from a small ecosystem of embedded evaluators with significant access to a large body of third-party auditors with greater independence but limited access. Our framework serves as a template that can be applied to different audit tasks and inform the degree of auditor authority.
items.title: Audits Need Access, Data, and Compute. But How Much?

items.summary: AI web agents can autonomously navigate websites and complete various tasks. As their capabilities and adoption expand, evaluating bot defenses requires adversarial stress tests. Although prior work demonstrates that existing agents can remain detectable, it remains unclear how effective bot defenses are against adversaries that coordinate evasion across browser fingerprints, automation controls, and interaction behavior. To investigate this threat, we introduce DarkAgent, an autonomous web agent that combines a forked Chromium browser that conceals automation artifacts and generative models that produce human-like mouse and keyboard traces. To address the limitations of existing keyboard mimickers, our keyboard model jointly generates realistic key events and their timings while reliably reproducing the target text. Released agent detectors accept our generated behavior as human, and trained classifiers find it substantially harder to distinguish from human traces than existing mimickers. DarkAgent achieves an 89% page-access bypass rate across a third-party stealth benchmark, exceeding the strongest published baseline by 12 percentage points. To further enhance the measurement of agents, we introduce a benchmark that measures browser fingerprints, interaction behavior, and network activity to assess each channel's contribution to detecting adversarial agents such as DarkAgent. On this benchmark, browser and behavioral modifications are complementary: either alone remains detectable, and only their combination evades all tested checks. Together, our findings expose the gap between passing existing bot defenses and reproducing human behavior, and point to timing between actions as a remaining signal for defenders.
items.title: Are Web Agents Still Detectable? Stress-Testing Bot Defenses with Coordinated Evasion

items.summary: While malware on platforms such as Windows and Android has been extensively studied, the macOS ecosystem remains comparatively understudied. To address this gap, we present MALET, a large-scale public dataset for macOS malware analysis. MALET contains 44{,}804 malicious Mach-O binaries and 44{,}457 samples with zero antivirus detections on VirusTotal. From the undetected set, we further identify 25{,}835 high-confidence benign samples using conservative, heuristic-based filtering. We also introduce Katalina, an open-source static analysis framework that extracts macOS-specific structural features and indicators of potential behavior at scale. Using MALET, we perform, to the best of our knowledge, the first large-scale static characterization of macOS malware. Our analysis reveals macOS-specific traits, including widespread misuse of security entitlements, abuse of native scripting interfaces, and irregularities in code-signing infrastructure. We find that 93.0\% of malicious samples are unsigned, demonstrating that unsigned code continues to execute in practice through user-mediated approval mechanisms. Among CA-signed malware, 28.4\% (816 samples) were associated with certificates that were later revoked, including samples publicly attributed to DPRK-linked threat actors, as reflected in antivirus labels and threat intelligence reports. Finally, we identify significant detection instability: in 185 structurally identical malicious samples, antivirus engines failed to provide consistent detections for 77.2\% (143 samples). Together, these results highlight persistent blind spots in macOS malware detection and motivate improved approaches to certificate abuse analysis, similarity-based clustering, and platform-specific defense mechanisms. Based on these insights, we outline concrete steps to advance the state of macOS malware analysis and defense.
items.title: MALET & Katalina: A Large-Scale Dataset and Static Analysis of macOS Malware

items.summary: Prediction markets are becoming an important mechanism for aggregating information and forecasting uncertain real-world events. As they grow in scale and value, reliable settlement becomes critical because settlement determines the winning outcome and allocation of market collateral. Yet many heterogeneous markets require market-specific evidence and interpretation, and incorrect settlement can create direct financial incentives for manipulation. In this paper, we ask how to settle heterogeneous markets correctly and efficiently at scale. We first compare existing settlement designs in their support for heterogeneous markets, reliance on direct operator intervention, and resistance to manipulation, motivating a layered architecture that combines incentivized crowdsourcing with stake-backed voting and selective post-settlement review. Building on this architecture, we develop a stake-backed settlement protocol that provides economic security and settlement liveness under market-specific verification costs. Specifically, we prove that manipulation is unprofitable for every settled market and give two constructions that support sufficient self-enforcing participation with controlled reward expenditure. Using historical Polymarket and UMA data, we evaluate the protocol under real-world conditions. We find that 99% of admitted markets can be settled with modest participation rewards even under high verification costs.
items.title: The Oracle Is Not Enough: Secure Settlement for Prediction Markets

items.summary: Third-party projects repackage free inference from LLM web applications and dedicated clients into independent APIs. We refer to such use beyond providers' permitted access, allocation, or redistribution conditions as LLM service freeloading (LSF). However, its scale and underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. We present a systematic measurement study of 513 open-source projects, tracing 1,588 inference paths across 64 upstream LLM services and characterizing their development, dependencies, and operating mechanisms. We find that 93.0% of repositories were created in 2026. Direct HTTP or WebSocket requests account for 83.2% of paths, making reproduction of product protocols the dominant invocation method. Projects adapt messages, reconstruct conversation state, and convert responses to support compatible APIs. Account selection or rotation appears on 304 paths (19.1%), allowing projects with multiple eligible accounts to distribute requests across their separate allowances. Our policy analysis finds that 58 of the 62 services with available terms explicitly prohibit at least one examined practice, including automated access, account sharing, or service redistribution. These restrictions cover both downstream API provision and the means of obtaining upstream inference. Our findings inform defenses against unauthorized consumption and redistribution of free LLM resources. We have responsibly disclosed our findings to the relevant providers.
items.title: Demystifying Real-world LLM Service Freeloading

items.summary: Rust crates confine unsafe code, such as calls into C or C++ libraries or system calls, behind safe interfaces that must uphold Rust's invariants. If an interface encodes one rule of the code beneath it too weakly, a program written in purely safe Rust can cause undefined behavior. Static analyzers and fuzzers are bound to fixed patterns or to the paths they execute. We propose LLM agents as auditors of these interfaces, and study how well they do it. We first define a taxonomy of the defects of such interfaces, including undefined behavior, divergences from the wrapped library, and incomplete unsafe contracts. We then measure, in repeated audits of a real-world crate by a closed and an open model, Claude Opus 5.5 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, which defect classes agents find, how well they triage them, and what makes them find more. Agents find the first two classes unprompted, but find few incomplete contracts even when asked. Their findings are almost always real, even without an independent reviewer, yet they lack triage discipline: they seldom confirm with a sanitizer, and they stop early. With the same guidance, the open model finds as many defects as the closed one at a quarter of the cost. We integrate these insights in Crustify, an agentic system for automating C-to-Rust tasks, and run it at scale. In 16 widely used crates, including the bindings to the C libraries OpenSSL, SQLite, libgit2, and libcurl and to the C++ engine V8, Crustify found 225 undefined-behavior bugs, 23 behavioral divergences, and 36 incomplete unsafe contracts, between 3 and 61 per crate at a median cost under $50 per audit. In the Linux kernel's Rust abstractions, it found 11 more undefined-behavior bugs and 4 incomplete contracts. Maintainers have fixed 26 of the 83 findings that we reported.
items.title: Agentic Discovery of Soundness Bugs in Safe Rust Bindings

items.summary: Users of large language model (LLM) services receive token bills with limited evidence of which calls incurred their charges. In broker-mediated agent workflows, calls arise after authorization and billing evidence spans service domains. A bill can count one genuine receipt twice and omit another. Valid metering evidence can also be attributed to the wrong execution. We present \textsc{TokenProv}, which uses authenticated provider acceptances to establish settlement coverage and verify token charges. An authenticated causal history links runtime attempts to the signed policy, and jointly signed handoffs bind intent, dispatch, and acceptance to the same call. Handoffs submitted independently of the bill can reveal omitted calls. The auditor requires a one-to-one match between observable acceptances and settled receipts. For each acceptance, a common provider relation binds metered usage to the cache-dependent execution of the accepted input using the registered model and serving rules, and checks the charge under the pricing rule. To limit serving-path overhead, providers can use attested state transitions in trusted execution environments or defer proof generation until audit by committing to witnesses in receipts before settlement. The auditor recomputes the bill from the verified charges. We prove audit soundness relative to authenticated evidence. Across five models, \textsc{TokenProv} with signed provider receipts achieves 94.4--107.4\% of baseline throughput with 54--66\,ms of online non-LLM processing per request. In a separate eight-call replay, deferring scoped proofs reduces foreground protocol time from 1.20\,s to 8.65\,ms (99.28\%). The auditor rejects all 1,600 validly signed attack queries across 100 adaptive episodes.
items.title: Where Did My Tokens Go? Verifiable Token Billing for LLM Services

items.summary: Brainprint authentication enables continuous identity verification, but EEG data are privacy-sensitive. Existing feature-level encrypted authentication (FLEA) schemes protect extracted features under a trusted-client assumption. We show theoretically and empirically that a compromised client with access to plaintext query features and continuous authentication scores can exactly recover a registered template after finitely many interactions. To address this risk, we propose TopoCryptoEEG, a homomorphic-encryption-based framework that encrypts preprocessed EEG data at the client and performs feature extraction, template matching, score computation, and threshold centering on ciphertexts at the server. This extends protection from extracted features to preprocessed EEG data and removes the client-side plaintext-feature interface exploited by the attack. For efficient encrypted authentication, we develop Multi-Window Topology-Aware Encoding (MWTE) and a Topographic Branch Model with Linear Fusion (TopoFuse-MLP) to preserve EEG spatial information while limiting multiplicative depth. Query-Patch Coordinate Packing (QPCP) and Lane-Preserving BSGS Evaluation (LP-BSGS) further reduce ciphertext operations. Experiments on HGD and BCICIV-2a show high authentication accuracy, with homomorphic computation taking 1-2 s on CPUs and about 14 ms on GPUs. TopoCryptoEEG achieves over 18x average speedup over the EER (IMWUT 2025) baseline, supporting practical privacy-preserving brainprint authentication.
items.title: TopoCryptoEEG: End-to-End Encrypted Framework for Brainprint Authentication

items.summary: LLM agents increasingly collaborate in group chats while holding tool access to confidential records, which makes the shared chat an attack surface. It remains unclear whether several colluding attackers extract such information more effectively than one. We introduce SwarmLeak, a red-teaming dataset of 24 synthetic group-chat scenarios across healthcare, law, finance, and software engineering, where attackers pose as colleagues to make a victim agent post protected fields despite an explicit confidentiality policy. With GLM 5.2 attacking five victim models through seven conversational strategies, we compare one attacker with a swarm of four sharing a private channel, matching scenarios, strategies, and a 200,000-token budget that also covers swarm coordination. Swarms show no advantage: a single attacker matches or exceeds them on every victim, and the share of runs leaking any field differs between conditions by at most 14.3 percentage points, whereas changing the victim shifts it from 0% to 99.4%. On the two most vulnerable models, nearly every run leaks under both conditions, but single attackers expose more of the record at first disclosure (85.4% vs. 68.1% of protected fields on Nemotron 3.5 Lightning). Four of the five victims leaked despite the policy. GLM 5.2 retrieved protected data in 64.3% of individual-attack runs and leaked in 0.6%: retrieval does not imply disclosure, but in high-stakes settings even one leaked field can identify a patient or client. At equal budgets, a larger red team is not automatically a stronger one; the victim model matters far more.
items.title: SwarmLeak: Does Coordination Improve Privacy Attacks on LLM Agents?

items.summary: Hyperdimensional computing (HDC) models deployed on edge hardware are valuable intellectual property that is easy to steal, since a trained classifier consolidates its learned knowledge into a compact set of class prototype hypervectors; yet protecting their ownership through watermarking remains largely unexplored. We present HDMark, the first model watermarking framework native to HDC, which encodes ownership in the same hyperdimensional algebra the model computes with. HDMark maps a multi-bit owner identity to secret quasi-orthogonal carriers, superimposes them holographically onto the trained class prototypes, and verifies ownership with a statistical test. Across four datasets and three HDC learning rules, HDMark leaves accuracy essentially unchanged and verifies a 64-bit identity in 99.8% of trials at p < 0.001. We derive closed-form expressions for prediction fidelity and bit recovery that match measurements within 0.4 pp mean absolute error. The watermark survives fine-tuning and low-bit quantization, while attempting to erase it through noise injection, pruning, or overwriting severely degrades model accuracy. We further identify a dimension-permutation attack specific to HDC, which reorders hypervector coordinates to evade verification without altering predictions, and counter it through encoder realignment. Finally, an AMD ZCU104 FPGA implementation confirms that HDMark adds no hardware overhead, remains bit-exact under aggressive undervolting, and stays verifiable under timing faults until the classifier itself fails.
items.title: HDMark: Holographic Multi-Bit Model Watermarking for Intellectual Property Protection in Hyperdimensional Computing

items.summary: Adversarial perturbation defenses protect images from unauthorized edits by adding imperceptible noise. Yet none of these methods have been evaluated against nudification, despite AI-generated non-consensual intimate imagery (AIG-NCII) being among the most documented harms of generative AI. Moreover, nudification edits are readily carried out through inpainting, the primary setting these protection methods are designed to defend against. We argue this is a problem-formulation failure since prior threat models do not correspond to nudification edits (also called attacks). The misalignment of existing approaches is structural, spanning mask shape, training and testing prompt distributions, and success criterion which causes existing evaluations to systematically overestimate protection effectiveness. We reformulate image protection against unauthorized editing around this documented harm. We introduce BODYBENCH, a benchmark of 648 fully synthetic clothed adult subjects, each paired with 11 mask variants spanning body, face, and context regions. We propose three harm-aligned metrics: sexualization, naturalness, and recognizability that jointly determine whether an inpainted output constitutes a successful nudification attack. Auditing four recent protection methods (PhotoGuard, DiffusionGuard, AdvPaint, DiffVax) on BODYBENCH, we find that protection succeeds in only one configuration of one method, and only under exact mask alignment between defender and attacker---a condition no real defender can guarantee and one that we show is easily always bypassed. We also show that standard evaluation metrics such as peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) are essentially uncorrelated with nudification protection. BODYBENCH makes this misalignment measurable and provides a foundation for defenses grounded in documented harm.
items.title: BODYBENCH: Evaluating Adversarial Image Defenses Against AI Nudification Inpainting

items.summary: The growing autonomy of AI agents in using external tools and making decisions has created an urgent need for comprehensive safety benchmarks. Existing benchmarks test compromised tool channels or adaptive multi-turn attacks, though they may not capture the unique capabilities of policy-governed tool-use agents, which must resist unauthorized requests without abandoning the legitimate work embedded in the same interaction. To fill this gap, we introduce TACT-Bench, a stateful benchmark built around scenario-specific stories, personas, manipulation tactics, and response-adaptive escalation. Each adversarial task targets an action explicitly prohibited by the policy provided to the assistant, while the policy remains hidden from the attacking user. TACT pairs each adversarial task with at least one benign counterpart, and its adversarial tasks retain authorized ground-truth actions when a compliant resolution remains available. We define these base tasks as TACT-Base. We additionally introduce TACT-TrustPrime, which places an independent benign task before an unrelated attack in the same conversation. We also propose Paired Selective Trustworthiness (PST), which combines explicit safe refusal with demonstrated capability on matched benign tasks, to analyze an agent's overcautiousness and practicality. Averaged across 6 different models as assistants, TACT-Base raises Attack-Induced Failure Rate (AFR) by 17.53% over four compatible attack baselines, and TACT-TrustPrime raises it by a further 17.01%. The two evaluated defense methods reduce AFR by only 8.35%--9.41% on average and do not consistently improve PST, underscoring the need for stronger policy-enforcement methods.
items.title: TACT-Bench: Testing Adaptive Conversational Threats against Tool-Use Agents

items.summary: Split-training privacy evaluations fail through distinct mechanisms. Evaluators can overlook an exposed gradient channel, align reconstructions against shifted labels, or deploy uncalibrated probes before testing a candidate defence, while calibrated attacks can also refute real defences. Separating these failure modes alters which claims survive. We conduct a retrospective evidentiary reanalysis across four split-LLM campaigns and two cross-cutting scope checks covering host key custody and variational mutual-information bounds, mapping every recorded claim to one of five admissibility states (breach, non-detection, undetermined coverage, invalid measurement, or out-of-scope inference). Across a 19-configuration exploration, only four of 24 required probes qualified, yet those four calibrated probes still established qualified privacy breaches in 13 configurations, while utility or learning-gain failures eliminated the remaining 6. In a seven-cell defence-redesign pilot, 2 quantised configurations failed utility gates, calibrated next-byte structure probes breached the 0.02 gate on all 7 cells (0.097 to 0.112), and qualified punctuation-property probes reached 0.79 to 0.89, yielding 4 failed and 3 undetermined composite privacy assessments (the latter from marginal null-band excursions on punctuation bindings). Negative evidence against both defence families remains intact. Scope checks further show that shared-key orthogonal wrappers protect passive network captures without hiding activations from a compromised restoring host, and why near-zero variational lower bounds leave worst-case leakage unconstrained. Rerunnable scripts verify 1,522 checks across 122 SHA-256-pinned artifacts while preserving each campaign's native seed intervals and retrospective boundaries.
items.title: Separating Measurement Failures from Defence Failures in Split Language-Model Privacy

items.summary: Vulnerability auditing of large C/C++ codebases is constrained by limited review attention. Human auditors and LLM-based agents need operational priors that indicate where to look first and what to suspect, but such priors are rarely available in directly usable form. Rather than proposing a new vulnerability detector, we derive audit-steering artifacts from evidence-backed root-cause analysis (RCA) reports. We introduce two complementary representations: Occurrence Context (OC), a location prior based on file role, function role, and data-structure class; and Vulnerability-Inducing Structural Patterns (VISP), reusable failure-mechanism priors. OC guides where to inspect, while VISP guides what to suspect. On 108 CVEs from Vul4C, OC's parser-based priority ranking, without LLM inference, outperforms generic prioritization baselines with moderate-to-large effect sizes. Packaged as executable SKILLs, OC and VISP form a dual-SKILL workflow that improves audit-relevant broad coverage, defined as match-or-partial findings within ground-truth functions that share the patch's failure mechanism, as assessed by three LLM judges. Across the 108-CVE cohort, dual-SKILL improves function-level broad matches by 5.3 percentage points; gains reach 7.2 points on mid-size projects and 15.0 points on large (1500-4999-line) vulnerable files. These results suggest that RCA-derived priors help direct limited audit attention toward vulnerable code. The agent-coverage evaluation is a single-run operational probe, with one run per commit, characterizing the direction and scale of the effect rather than its precise magnitude.
items.title: Mixed-Initiative Mining of Root-Cause Analyses into Audit Priors for C/C++ Vulnerability Hunting

items.summary: As mobile health advances, the use of biomedical sensors for disease monitoring, diagnosis, and treatment is increasing. These sensors often need to be connected through wireless communication technologies to process physiological information from various body parts effectively. Since the data transmitted in these devices usually contain sensitive personal medical information, it is crucial to establish secure communication between devices. In recent studies, the inter-pulse intervals between heartbeats are often used as the key source. They can be extracted from physiological signals such as photoplethysmogram (PPG) or electrocardiogram (ECG), allowing key agreement schemes without pre-key distribution. However, traditional solutions are based on contact measurement devices (e.g., wristbands, chest straps), which limit their applicability in contactless healthcare scenarios. In this paper, we propose a remote PPG-based key agreement scheme to facilitate secure communication between contactless medical devices. We leverage medical devices equipped with cameras to capture remote PPG signals from human faces, and then utilize the signal's power spectral density and peak-peak interval to establish a key agreement with signals synchronously acquired in the Body Area Network (BAN). We have carried out performance evaluations on three publicly available datasets to demonstrate the feasibility of our proposed scheme. In addition, we have also presented a comprehensive proof of the security of our proposed scheme.
items.title: SigK: rPPG-based key agreement scheme for mHealth

items.summary: Apple ships hundreds of task-specific machine-learning models inside iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and tvOS. We present, to our knowledge, the first systematic security analysis of this on-device surface. We harvested 1,137 CoreML artifacts from six platform images and two device harvests, and a conversion pipeline recovered 155 previously opaque bundles as loadable mlpackage archives. Eight findings. (1) 368 of 1,137 artifacts expose plaintext learned parameters (281 blobs, 369.61 MiB) and 166 of 166 MIL bundles leak internal model-database tokens. (2) Specification versions 1-9 coexist and locale variants diverge architecturally. (3) Across 82,092 adversarial evaluations (221 model paths), worst-case flip rates reach 100%; zero-width spaces flip 65% of the Indian-English and 70% of the US-English SMS filter. (4) A 16-byte weight edit flips 7 of 8 probe inputs of a system model, with no runtime integrity check observed. (5) Loading Apple's own hand-gesture model crashes libBNNS through the public CoreML API (4/4 on production M2, also macOS 27.0); Apple ruled it a self-crash outside the security boundary. (6) Eleven bundles ship isUpdatable=1 hooks. (7) SMS text-classifier latency is 13.1-52.0 ms, 92.4% in the CPU-side NLP core, not the ANE. (8) The classifiers label 8-9 of 10 phishing messages Transactional. We filed three reports with Apple Product; all were declined as not crossing a security boundary, and we report the findings as robustness results.
items.title: Harvesting Apple's Orchard: A Security Analysis of On-Device CoreML Models Across the Apple Ecosystem

items.summary: ERCOT publishes every generator's hourly offer curve 60 days after the operating day. Market monitors, researchers and traders use these records to study the merit order and check for withholding. PJM publishes the same kind of data with unit names replaced by codes, on the view that masking keeps offers confidential. We test that view on ERCOT data from 2024 to 2026, where names are public and so provide ground truth, by masking the records under PJM's published rules. Public EIA and EPA data match 25% of the masked units we can score (32% of their capacity) to their plant, and 45% fall within the top five guesses. PJM's feed carries the same fields, so we expect masking to fail there too. Publishing exact fuel-group totals instead does not help. An attacker who knows the other units in a group recovers one unit's high-price offers exactly, and an outsider who knows only the target's outage dates reaches a correlation of 0.77, most of it from a few renewable and hydro units that offer at very high prices (0.32 over fossil units). We propose a differentially private release: monthly totals by fuel group and price bin, with Gaussian noise calibrated under zero-concentrated differential privacy so that each unit's whole year of offers is protected. It publishes an unbiased noisy layer and derives a monotone supply curve and shares from it at no extra privacy cost. At $\varepsilon=10$ per unit-year the market supply curve stays within 11% of the truth, the implied clearing price within \$3.0/MWh, and the attacker's correlation falls to 0.23. Whether an analysis still works depends on one ratio, how much the true quantity varies month to month against the noise, which predicts the accuracy of totals to within 0.05. The clearing price, supply slope and combined-cycle capacity remain usable, but no monthly release, private or exact, can answer questions about single hours or single units.
items.title: Your bids are showing: re-identifying power plants in anonymized market data, and a differentially private alternative

items.summary: Radio frequency fingerprint identification (RFFI) is a promising device authentication technique for the Internet of Things (IoT) that leverages hardware impairments to uniquely identify devices. However, most existing RFFI systems operate under a closed-set assumption and lack the ability to detect rogue devices, which poses significant security risks. In this paper, we propose an open-set RFFI approach that jointly performs rogue device detection and legitimate device classification. Specifically, we designed a multi-task RFFI system that integrates an autoencoder (AE) for rogue device detection and a fully connected (FC) layer for classification. To enrich the feature representation, we generated two channel-independent spectrograms (CISs) with distinct window lengths from the I/Q signals, capturing complementary time-frequency characteristics. These CISs were processed in parallel by two Vision Transformer (ViT) networks, and their outputs were fused via feature concatenation to construct a device fingerprint for both tasks. We built a testbed involving ten legitimate LoRa devices and five rogue devices. We conducted a comprehensive experimental evaluation and compared our approach with several benchmark algorithms. Experimental results show that our fused feature multi-task RFFI consistently outperformed the baselines in both legitimate device classification and rogue device detection. Our proposed approach achieved an accuracy of 91.1% and an area under the curve (AUC) of over 0.72 in a realistic wireless scenario where the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) was 20 to 30 dB.
items.title: Open-Set Radio Frequency Fingerprint Identification with Feature Fusion and Vision Transformer

items.summary: This article presents a technical and theoretical assessment of the Quantum-Entangled Neuro-Symbolic Swarm Federation (QENSSF), a framework intended for privacy-preserving, quantum-secure, AI-powered, multimodal healthcare data analysis, introduced by Ben Othman and Ali (2025). They claim QENSSF is a first-in-class framework with provable privacy and security guarantees, support these with theorems and proofs, report an experimental evaluation on IBM's quantum Eagle processor, report a real-world quantum key distribution (QKD) test, and claim use of real-world multimodal datasets (ADNI, UK Biobank, and MIMIC-IV). Our examination of quantitative support for these claims identified various concerns. Most importantly, the security criterion of a central guarantee (Theorem 1) cannot be satisfied given the risk formulation and relevant constraints, which, along with calculation errors in the proof, directly undermines the claim of provable security. Furthermore, insufficient reporting of biomedical datasets and unresolved discrepancies in the hardware evaluation limit verification of the experimental claims and overall reproducibility. QENSSF identifies a real need: ensuring privacy and security of healthcare data while patients benefit from AI-powered analysis. This need is particularly pressing for sensitive neural data, including the neuroimaging data available through sources such as ADNI. Privacy concerns also extend to wearable EEG data, for which reidentification risks can persist despite deidentification. However, QENSSF's foundational inconsistencies need resolution before it could be considered in the neurosecurity domain.
items.title: Internal inconsistencies and unresolved experimental evidence in a quantum neurosecurity framework

items.summary: LLM-based security review agents can reason about vulnerabilities that deterministic tools miss, but deploying them responsibly requires knowing whether they actually work. Existing benchmarks construct ground truth synthetically or from public CVE databases and are blind to the vulnerability patterns specific to a given production codebase. We present an evaluation framework grounded in an organisation's own vulnerabilities, with three contributions. First, a dataset construction methodology that derives ground truth from operational security data (bug bounty reports, penetration test findings and internally reported vulnerabilities), exploiting the property that a confirmed vulnerability must exist immediately before its fix is merged and be absent immediately after. Second, two complementary evaluation strategies: one reviewing the pull request that introduced a vulnerability and one searching a repository where it already exists. Both run through a two-agent pipeline pairing a Security Engineer agent, which reviews code without knowledge of the vulnerability, with a Judge agent that decides whether its findings would have mitigated the known issue. Third, a trace-level behavioural characterisation of how frontier models reason about these vulnerabilities. Across GPT-5.5, Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.7, GPT-5.5 shows higher discovery rates on the pull-request strategy (57%, 95% CI [42%, 72%]) after a round of OPRO-style improvements, and Sonnet 4.6 on the repository strategy (69%, 95% CI [56%, 81%]). Trace analysis shows the models have complementary strengths that explain these differences, and that outcome-only scoring can mischaracterise their production behaviour. The methodology relies only on artefacts that vulnerability management workflows commonly produce, though all results come from a single organisation's codebase and we have not tested how well they generalise.
items.title: Evaluating LLM Security Review Agents with Operationally Sourced Ground Truth

items.summary: Most resource estimates for breaking secp256k1 with Shor's algorithm describe one long run per attempt, and the spacetime volume of that run, its peak number of logical qubits times its Toffoli count, sets its logical-error budget. Ekerå's tradeoff shrinks each run by using more runs, but how far it can shrink the largest run, and at what circuit cost, has not been determined. We minimize the volume of the largest run while every key is recovered with probability at least 0.99, within ten times the total volume of three runs of Häner et al.\ and $2^{40}$ classical operations. We prove that a linear run fixed in advance, which starts its group register at a point and discards its label, reveals at most $\log_2(1+(|S|-1)/r)$ bits about a uniform key, where $|S|$ counts its exponent values and $r$ is the group order. With generic post-processing and the baseline's window costs, splitting alone then shrinks the largest run at most 1.86 times within the budget. To gain more, we make each exponent bit cheaper with windows that share one table point among exponent values related by six symmetries of the curve, on a point-addition core borrowed from the ECDSA.Fail leaderboard. One random scalar and one random start per run give every approximate addition uniform operands, and a bound on each run's outcomes certifies, for every key, a decoder that discards flagged runs. We count every Toffoli gate and every qubit of every run, and each configuration solved all 563 of its pre-registered simulated trials on secp256k1. The best one shrinks the largest run 3.87 times at 8.79 times the baseline's total volume, against 2.81 times for Ekerå's tradeoff on the same core, and its run is at least 2.6 times smaller than every design of Initio Intelligence.
items.title: How Small Can a Single Shor Run Be? Limits and Constructions for secp256k1

items.summary: Android kernels have long suffered from slow patch propagation from Linux upstream, with fixes often reaching devices far later than conventional Linux distributions. Until recently, this lag was largely a patch-management problem. With rapidly improving LLM agents, it is becoming an exploitation problem: public upstream patches can now serve as blueprints for building working n-day exploits before downstream devices are fixed. We test this threat end to end by building an automated pipeline that screens upstream Linux patches, reproduces memory-safety vulnerabilities on Android targets, and drives an LLM agent to construct local privilege escalation exploits from an untrusted application. Across 152 candidate CVEs reported over 33 months, we reproduce 38 vulnerabilities and generate 17 independently verified exploits under production defenses. Exploitation takes a median of 14.3 agent-hours and $321 in API cost, with 90% median reliability; 12 of 14 trials succeed on Pixel 9 and Pixel 10 devices. Notably, the pipeline relies only on publicly available, off-the-shelf models. Surprisingly, only 3 of the 17 exploited CVEs appear in Android Security Bulletins, suggesting limited visibility into which upstream fixes address vulnerabilities that affect Android kernels. For these 17 CVEs, the corresponding upstream patches reach Pixel devices with a median delay of 181 days. Together, these results reveal a stark asymmetry: attackers can increasingly automate exploitation in hours, while defenders still identify and deploy fixes on the timescale of months.
items.title: Aftershock: Yesterday's Linux Kernel Bugs, Tomorrow's Android Exploits

items.summary: A coding agent may need to upload a report while its sandbox blocks network access. A host mediator can restore delivery, but an injected instruction may add a secret to the approved request. We study this interaction using files and HTTP receipts to measure effects independently of control logs. Two prospective frozen-input cohorts comprise 110 and 300 runs on previously explored authored tasks. Restrictive sandboxing produces no observed attack harm but reduces benign utility to 6/8 and 12/24. Mediation restores uploads and admits disclosure; complete-line matching retains full benign utility but misses two value-only disclosures in the expanded cohort. A separate 72-run boundary study identifies encoded disclosure, observer misses, and formatting checks that obscure benign refusals. An 80-run SafeAgents/OpenShell follow-up shows that containment stops the tested guard misses among valid observations, while mediation restores benign uploads and delivers both encoded-attestation attacks. Twelve judge-error rows remain unscored. A separate response-capture diagnostic reproduces their failures at the native token budget. A 12-run exact-publication-contract experiment blocks both attacks but also rejects both benign formatting variants; a 4-run normalized follow-up restores both benign uploads while still rejecting both attacks. These small, single-model studies identify delivery-path and measurement limits; they do not establish general attack resistance.
items.title: Where Agent Defenses Fail: A Case Study of Policy Compositions and Measurement Limits

items.summary: Recent research has investigated fair transaction ordering in blockchain consensus. An orthogonal line of work has demonstrated that equipping replicas with trusted execution environments (TEEs) enables more efficient consensus protocols with only $2f{+}1$ replicas. In this work, we bridge these two areas and demonstrate that two key fair-ordering properties, ordering linearizability and $γ$-batch-order fairness with minimal batching, cannot be implemented in partially synchronous networks with $2f{+}1$ replicas, even when the replicas are equipped with TEEs. We show that Byzantine replicas can circumvent TEE protections by manipulating the timing of transaction submissions to the enclave, thereby biasing the resulting ordering indicators. However, we prove that assuming a synchronous network allows both properties to be implemented with a reduced replica count. We propose two mechanisms: one uses absolute TEE-attested timestamps to guarantee ordering linearizability in a system of $n \ge 2f{+}1$ replicas, and the other uses TEE-maintained relative sequence numbers to guarantee $γ$-batch-order fairness when $n > \frac{2γf}{2γ-1}$. Ultimately, we integrate these mechanisms into a synchronous lane-based consensus algorithm, achieving strong fair-ordering properties and superior performance while requiring fewer replicas than representative state-of-the-art baselines.
items.title: Pearl: TEE-Enabled Fair Ordering with Minimal Replication

items.summary: Black-box integrity verification aims to detect unauthorized modifications to outsourced models using only prediction APIs. Existing frameworks seek to improve verification efficiency through sensitive fingerprints: queries whose predictions are more likely to change under tampering than those of genuine inputs. We show that this sensitivity can also help dishonest providers recognize verification queries and selectively conceal tampering. We prove that excess sensitivity relative to genuine inputs lower-bounds statistical distinguishability. We evaluate five integrity verification frameworks across three model architectures, three datasets, and three adversarial knowledge settings. When the deployed framework is known, our fingerprint detectors achieve AUCs at least 0.989, and selective filtering makes all five frameworks require significantly larger estimated query budgets than genuine inputs, reversing their intended efficiency advantage. A query-efficiency advantage remains marginally in a small subset of evaluated settings with poor detection transfer. We further design verification methods under stronger concealment constraints but find that reduced detectability comes with losses in sensitivity or fingerprint-generation success. Our results expose a sensitivity-detectability tension and show that sensitivity alone does not ensure efficient black-box verification against adaptive malicious providers.
items.title: The Fingerprinting Paradox: Why Sensitivity Undermines Black-Box Model Integrity Verification

items.summary: Tutors built on large language models (LLMs) are told not to give away answers, but a learner does not have to ask for the answer all at once. Existing safeguards judge each reply within the current conversation, so a learner can open a new session, reword the problem, or request a worked solution to the same problem with different numbers. We call this cross-session disclosure and propose a defense: a persistent, per-learner disclosure ledger. For every problem a learner brings, the system builds a typed solution graph. Before a reply is released, a gate matches the reply's own content, not the learner's wording, against the ledger by result values and by type-labeled solution structure, then computes which steps the learner could now derive. The reply is withheld if that set reaches the final answer or exceeds a budget. In a simulation of 3,000 problems, the ledger reduced leakage through renumbered practice variants from 100% to 10.6% while honest learners completed 94-99.5% of problems. With two real LLM tutors (Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Phi-3.5-mini-instruct) on 60 problems, leakage through renumbered variants fell from 0.58 to 0.08 and from 1.00 to 0.18, with 98% honest completion. The ledger did not reduce split requests beyond a per-session gate in the live runs. All acceptance criteria were fixed before each run.
items.title: Leaks by Installments: Cross-Session Answer Disclosure in LLM Tutors and a Ledger-Based Defense

items.summary: We study how to represent and randomize points in $d$-dimensional Euclidean space to obtain accurate bipartite matchings under metric privacy. Given $n$ private and $n$ public points, we analyze local mechanisms that randomize each private point or its distances to the public points. Using the public points' affine span, we construct a smaller representation that preserves all matching costs. When a trusted server receives the private points, we establish privacy and utility guarantees for Gumbel matching, which randomizes edge costs and releases only the assignment. Through upper bounds and worst-case constructions, we establish the tight rate $Θ\!\left(n\min\{d,\log n\}/\varepsilon\right)$ for expected cost above the nonprivate optimum. Benchmark experiments support $d\approx\log n$ as a practical guide to the transition between directly randomizing point coordinates and using Gumbel matching. Extensions to squared Euclidean costs enable private nonparametric two-sample hypothesis testing. These results show how the application's trust model guides representation and dimension choices for better utility: under local privacy, low-dimensional point representations reduce excess cost, while under central privacy, distance representations achieve the optimal rate even in high dimension.
items.title: Matching Under Metric Privacy

items.summary: We study message authentication over a public channel against a computationally unbounded adversary. Motivated by low-complexity applications, we consider schemes that leverage off-the-shelf binary linear codes already used for error correction in communication systems. Existing code-based constructions derive an authentication tag primarily from a single symbol in a $q$-ary code, which limits the tag length. However, selecting several binary coordinates allows a fixed binary linear code to support different tag lengths. We characterize how coordinate selection and ordering affect the statistical guarantees against impersonation and substitution attacks. In particular, we explore three methods: the subset selector, the ordered selector, and the independent selector. They read uniformly chosen coordinates in a fixed public or a secret random order, or with replacement, and add a uniform mask. With a fresh key per message, all three achieve the optimal impersonation probability $2^{-l_t}$ for $l_t$-bit tags. We bound the subset selector's substitution probability using only nonzero weights. Those of the other two depend only on the code length $n$, $l_t$, and the nonzero weight farthest from $n/2$. The independent selector achieves $2^{-l_t}$ for substitution when all nonzero weights equal $n/2$. Finally, we evaluate first-order Reed-Muller and Bose-Chaudhuri-Hocquenghem dual subcodes.
items.title: Code-Based Message Authentication with Statistical Guarantees via Coordinate Selection and Masking

items.summary: Model alignment is the primary safety and security mechanism for enforcing refusal of malicious prompts in modern foundation models; yet, existing adversarial evaluations implicitly assume underlying hardware integrity. In this paper, we present FATCAT, the first physical fault-injection attacks capable of eliminating refusal in modern large language and vision-language models. Specifically, we present a non-invasive electromagnetic (EM) fault injection attack targeting GPU-accelerated Systems-on-Chip with physical access, requiring neither software execution privileges nor model-layer access. By leveraging an autonomous Radio Frequency (RF) side-channel trigger to synchronize EM faults to the prompt prefill phase, the attack corrupts safety-critical memory transactions across off-chip LPDDR5 DRAM and on-chip LPDDR physical interfaces without crashing the system while preserving model coherence. Evaluated on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and AGX Thor running Llama 3.2 1B and Gemma 3 1B, localized physical faults reliably force models to fulfill restricted requests, demonstrating that model-level alignment provides no robust security guarantees without hardware-level fault tolerance. Finally, we demonstrate the physical-world consequences of this vulnerability on an active 6-DoF robotic manipulator controlled by a SmolVLA vision-language-action policy. Our attack silently corrupts the model forcing the arm into abrupt, hazardous lunges; in two instances the robotic arm attempted to pinch the paper author -- proving that hardware faults can directly translate into real physical harm.
items.title: FATCAT: Fault Injection Attacks Targeting Chip-level Alignment

items.summary: An audit recorder must permit exact recovery with a small private index before it knows which questions a future reader will ask. A recursion on question partitions generates the decision trees, their eventwise costs and the price equations. A common-optimal-tree criterion explains when reduction to a fractional cover preserves the result. On uniform binary linear event spaces with four private roles, if every quartet is split evenly by some bit, optimal identification probability at expected follow-up budget $b$ is $(1+b)/2$. Otherwise it is $\min(1/2+b/3,3/4)$. We characterize all priors attaining the latter curve in its rising regime and derive a closed-form compiler for three binary fields. For a population tilted by one pairwise parity we obtain the full budget curve and a single recorder attaining it. On eight negotiated TLS suites the aligned populations allow a 60 percent follow-up rate at a 70 percent identification ceiling. A pairwise correlation with unchanged marginal field frequencies reduces that maximum to 40 percent. Across 960 local TLS sessions, the recorder recovered every negotiated suite using two private bits per session.
items.title: The Privacy Cost of Writing an Audit Receipt Before Its Context Is Known

items.summary: Software dependencies execute within the trust boundary of downstream applications, yet provenance, static analysis, and package-level behavioral approaches do not directly determine how a released artifact behaves for a specific program. We present Preflight, a program-scoped pre-execution verifier for Python dependencies that extracts application-referenced symbols, iteratively synthesizes and validates function-level harnesses, executes resolved artifacts in a restricted environment, records behavioral fingerprints, and compares target behavior against prior versions when suitable baselines exist. We evaluate Preflight on four real software-supply-chain incidents under five application contexts, a 100-package benign corpus, and a controlled function-level versus import-only ablation. Preflight returns malicious verdicts in four incident contexts and a clean verdict in the LiteLLM client context, where the affected proxy-server path is not exercised. All 100 evaluated benign packages receive clean verdicts, with zero observed false positives. In a controlled ablation on Ultralytics and ctx, function-level harnesses expose malicious behavior in both incidents, whereas import-only probing exposes neither. Together, these results show that conditioning behavioral verification on the downstream program can expose security-relevant dependency behavior while remaining selective on benign workloads.
items.title: Preflight: Agentic Last-Mile Verification for AI Software Supply Chains

items.summary: Runtime controls for tool-using agents depend on manifests that state what each tool may read and where its output may go. Evaluations of these controls, including ChainCaps, report per-attack blocking: the share of attacks a set of manifests stops. We show that this is the wrong unit. A catalog is only as safe as its weakest source policy: if $M$ independently authored policies are each wrong with probability $p$, the chance that the catalog contains an accepted exfiltration path is $1-(1-p)^M$, while per-attack blocking stays at $1-p$. Three lines of evidence agree. In synthetic catalogs run through two enforcement engines, ChainCaps and OpenAPPA, per-attack blocking holds at 92% while catalog vulnerability rises from 22% at 10 tools to 99% at 200, and composition provides no protective effect. A fifteen-model authoring pilot shows that real errors cluster by author, so a 200-tool catalog behaves like about 5 independent decisions rather than 60 (95% interval 3.4 to 9.2). On 114 real MCP tools with expert-written rules, the models' own manifests block 89% of attacks yet leave 9 of 15 catalogs open, as the author-effect model predicts and independence does not. Evaluations should report catalog vulnerability, the sink coverage of their tests, and an effective number of independent decisions alongside per-attack blocking.
items.title: Per-Attack Blocking Hides Catalog Vulnerability: A Weakest-Link Analysis of Tool Manifests

items.summary: Modern commodity DPI systems are capable of analyzing packet sizes, directions, and timings to detect circumvention tools even when those tools use sophisticated obfuscation. The anti-censorship community has called for innovation in traffic shaping and built an ecosystem that facilitates the adoption of new shaping techniques. However, a fundamental gap is halting progress: \textit{what} should circumvention traffic look like? Past experience with traffic shaping has underscored that effective shaping must produce traffic that looks like legitimate Internet traffic while limiting the ability of censors to identify multiple proxies through shared fingerprints. In this paper, we use our access to large-scale real-world TLS traffic at a regional ISP to analyze approximately 12 million connections, finding that individual servers differ substantially from the broader TLS population and that traffic patterns vary across services. Combining these empirical observations with past experience with traffic shaping, we build CenShaper, which shapes each proxy's traffic to look like a selected TLS server. To reproduce these server-specific patterns, CenShaper trains a shared generative model using traffic from TLS connections to many servers and adapts it for each proxy using a small sample of recorded connections to its selected server. Our model evaluation shows that fingerprints learned from known proxies transfer poorly to proxies imitating previously unseen TLS services. In end-to-end testing, CenShaper reduces the detection rate of TLS-over-TLS fingerprinting from over 85\% to approximately 3\% at a 1\% false positive rate. Finally, we show how running CenShaper as a sidecar process simplifies integration with existing circumvention tools, making it a practical defense against increasingly powerful traffic analysis attacks.
items.title: CenShaper: Shaping Proxy Traffic for Censorship Circumvention

items.summary: Recent incidents involving agents bypassing sandboxing and network isolation have raised concerns about existing agent harnesses, prompting frontier labs such as OpenAI to reevaluate the security of their training platforms. Incident reviews show that determined agents can escape processes, containers, and VMs, or bypass their isolation through advanced side and covert channels. Follow-up audits also found that some agents concealed their actions by disabling monitoring and tampering with logs. We propose Airlock, an architecture that pairs each agent's VM with an Airlock VM, each running in a separate hardware-isolated Trusted Execution Environment (TEE). The Airlock VM fully mediates the agent's interactions with the outside world, including network and storage operations. We modify the firmware layer of Arm's Confidential Computing Architecture, Realm Management Monitor (RMM), and the kernels of both VMs so that the Airlock VM serves the agent VM's IO without involving the host. We adapt OpenShell, an agent runtime supporting sandboxing and governance policies, to this architecture. Airlock keeps network and filesystem policies, and credential protection effective even if the agent VM is fully compromised, and it removes the host from the agent's IO path, reducing opportunities for collusion and covert channels with the host. Finally, we extend the Airlock VM's capabilities to provide tamper-proof auditing of all agent operations, preserving forensic evidence even if the Airlock VM is compromised. We implement and evaluate Airlock on a Radxa development board. Our evaluation shows a loss of filesystem performance and network latency for small messages under 15% and a drop of network bandwidth by half or more, which in practice has a limited effect on typical agent tasks.
items.title: Airlock: Robust Sandboxing and Governance of Rogue Agents

items.summary: Agent skills are reusable packages that extend a large language model (LLM) agent with scripts, third-party dependencies, and natural-language instructions. An agent builds a skill's arguments from user requests and untrusted external content, so a flaw left by a benign author can escalate a prompt injection to code execution. Existing studies target malicious skills or a single attack vector, and none tests whether an agent can reach such flaws. We present the first registry-scale empirical study of the supply chain attack surface arising from unintentional vulnerabilities in agent skills, over all 48,682 skills in ClawHub. The study covers two carried-over risks, dependencies and first-party code, and two agent-native ones, install instructions and credentials printed to stdout. We screen all skills by static analysis, manually review all 3,428 cases flagged by the four main detectors, and test reachability by running sampled flagged skills in a sandbox and with a live LLM agent under indirect prompt injection. First, dependency risk carries over in a different form: 49.6% of the skills with resolvable dependencies depend on a version with a known CVE, and unlike npm packages, which mostly become vulnerable after release, 78.3% of them are born vulnerable, already exposed at publication. Second, few of these CVEs are reachable: agent input reaches the vulnerable function in only 3.0% of the affected skills, whereas 21 of 22 sampled first-party flaws are exploited end to end in the sandbox. Third, a live agent executes the injected payload in 48.5% of the sampled flagged skills, but almost always in its own shell before the skill runs, and the payload reaches a flaw in the skill itself in only 5.0%. Hence, registries should prioritize first-party flaws over dependency alerts, and agent runtimes should not pass skill arguments through a shell.
items.title: Carried-Over and Agent-Native Threats in the Supply Chain of LLM Agent Skills
